abertura: Flip a coin and it lands heads 10 times in a row, you're gonna tell yourself the next one's gotta be tails. But the coin doesn't remember what it landed on.
transcricao: Flip a coin and it lands heads 10 times in a row, you're gonna tell yourself the next one's gotta be tails. But the coin doesn't remember what it landed on. Psychology calls this the gambler's fallacy. Your brain expects things to even out. You lose twice in a row and you think the third one's gotta be a guaranteed win. Or months go by with everything going great so you start waiting for something to get bad. But reality doesn't keep score the way your brain does. And it's not just coins, it's life too. You tell yourself, I've sold for so much, I've been patient for so long, I've waited so long, it's my turn for things to feel easy. But the world doesn't owe you anything. Just because you've been through a lot doesn't mean there's a day coming where it all turns around for you. The truth is, love doesn't remember your past, and life doesn't owe you fairness just because you went through something hard. Welcome to the other side.

legenda: what nobody wants to accept about politics
abertura: If you're on the left, you probably think right-wing voters are less informed than you. If you're on the right, you probably think left-wing voters are naive.
transcricao: If you're on the left, you probably think right-wing voters are less informed than you. If you're on the right, you probably think left-wing voters are naive. And after an election disclosed, like in my home country of Brazil, both sides are doing it at the same time, and it's called naive realism. Here's how this works. You feel like you see the world exactly as it is, not a version of it. You don't see your take as your take. You see it as reality. So you figure any reasonable person with the same information has to agree with you, right? And if they don't, then something's wrong with them. They're dumb, they're acting in bad faith, or their ideology is messing up with their head. And this has actually been tested. After 9-11, psychologists gave people five options on how the U.S. should react. From all-out war to diplomacy only. People saw their own option as the logic one. The further an option was from theirs, the more they blamed bad judgment. Then they asked how likely the participants were to make mistakes on their own judgment. And people said they were way less likely than the average person, and their co-workers, even than strangers at the airport. That's called the blind spot bias. You spot everyone else's bias easily, but your own you barely do. So you put those together and you get two sides that are each sure that the other one is the problem. That doesn't make every position equal. The facts still exist, but feeling certain doesn't mean that you're actually right. You can be wrong with total conviction and that oftentimes happens. So before you decide someone who disagrees with you is uninformed, dishonest or naive, maybe they're just seeing something from where they stand that you can't see from where you stand. Be more tolerant and welcome to the other side.

abertura: Some of the most intelligent people I've ever met in my life are the ones who ask a lot of questions. They get hyped up, they get excited, they have like this childish energy to them.
transcricao: Some of the most intelligent people I've ever met in my life are the ones who ask a lot of questions. They get hyped up, they get excited, they have like this childish energy to them. And deep down, I know they're actually so intelligent and I can always discuss emotional topics with them and they're going to understand and connect with me on that. On the other hand, the people who pretend to be mature and serious all the time are usually dumb. You know why that is? I think it's because with intelligence, it comes being a little childish because children are the ones who like ask a lot of questions all the time. And in their learning or development phases, they're the ones who just pick your brain all the time. So I think if you're actually looking to become smarter or increase your knowledge or wisdom, maybe try picking up that childish behavior. And knowledge comes from embarrassment, from not knowing. What would you rather have? Knowledge that will stay for you for the rest of your life or a little bit of embarrassment that you'll forget about 10 minutes from now? Welcome to the other side.

legenda: what if chasing pleasure is the whole point of being alive?

abertura: What's the difference between being confident and never doubting yourself? Nietzsche says very few people truly have confidence in themselves.
transcricao: What's the difference between being confident and never doubting yourself? Nietzsche says very few people truly have confidence in themselves. Some never doubt, some doubt all the time. And you would think the ones that never doubt have more confidence. They move forward, they seem solid. But Nietzsche disagrees with that. Most people who never doubt themselves are just blind to whatever could make them doubt. He calls this the useful blindness. They never see the uncertainty, so they don't have to answer to it. Then there are the people who doubt. They see their limits and the chance that they'll fail. They've got a skeptic inside of them asking, what if you can't do it? For them, confidence isn't given, it's conquered. And everything good they do becomes an argument against this skeptic. They don't kill the doubt, they answer it. So confidence and doubt are two sides of the same coin. There's no ultimate confidence that can never be attacked. It only exists in the face of doubt. You can go a step further. The peak confidence is going looking for what could prove you wrong. You don't gain confidence by protecting yourself from tests. You gain it from testing yourself. So ask yourself, can I doubt myself without it shaking me? If the answer is yes, you're probably not somebody who never doubts. You just understood you didn't need to be certain to be confident. Welcome to the other side.

legenda: do you still think you're not enough?

transcricao: I am not enough. I had a thought that I'm not enough. I'm noticing a thought that I'm not enough. What evidence is there that I'm not enough? I am not this distortion that my thoughts are telling me that I am. I can let the thought that I'm not enough go.

abertura: What if I told you not everybody lives at the same level of consciousness? They say there are seven levels of consciousness and most people don't even make it past the first.
transcricao: What if I told you not everybody lives at the same level of consciousness? They say there are seven levels of consciousness and most people don't even make it past the first. Level one, you live within the system, you work, you consume, you repeat. You don't question anything, you just play the game. You're an autopilot. Level two, something starts to feel off. The news, your routine, all the noise. It just doesn't make sense to you, but you still can't explain why. Level three, you start questioning everything. Politics, religion, even science. You start thinking for yourself and people start calling you crazy. Level 4. You start seeing the manipulation. You realize the system shapes your mind through music, movies, other people, and fear. Level 5. You stop blaming everything outside of yourself. You start looking inward and you realize that your emotions and patterns have been shaping your reality this whole time. Level 6. You become intentional. You start taking control of your energy and consciously shaping your life through what you focus on, what you believe in, and what you allow to stay in your mind. level seven you become grateful for the experience you understand that nothing outside of you is going to save you because you realize the power was inside of you all along and if any of this somehow made sense to you congratulations welcome to the other side
